cards.text: Jacob, Isaac's son, has been working for Laban, his father-in-law, for years (Genesis 29:20, 30). Rachel, one of Jacob's wives, has given birth to a son named Joseph. After that, Jacob walks up to Laban with something on his mind.

cards.question: Jacob has something to ask his father-in-law Laban. What is it?

answers.text: Send him on his way back home
Give him a field of his own
Let him build a house nearby

cards.question: Jacob plans to leave his wives and children behind with Laban and go home alone.

cards.text: Laban is NOT ready to let him go. He says, "If I have found favor in your eyes, please stay."

cards.question: Laban says he has learned by divination that the LORD has ___ him because of Jacob.

cards.text: Then Laban says, "Name your wages, and I will pay them." Friend, when the boss says NAME YOUR PRICE, you don't blink, you don't cough, you don't check your phone, you start TALKING.
And Jacob TALKS. He reminds Laban how he has served him and how Laban's livestock have thrived under his care, like a man walking into his yearly review with a folder full of receipts.

cards.question: Jacob tells Laban that he had very little before Jacob arrived, but now his wealth has increased many times over.

cards.text: Then Jacob asks, "But now, when may I also provide for my own household?" And Laban asks, "What can I give you?"

cards.question: Jacob says Laban doesn't need to give him anything. He'll keep shepherding Laban's flocks if Laban does one thing. What does Jacob want as his wages?

answers.text: Spotted or speckled animals and dark-colored lambs
The pure white sheep and goats
A tenth of every new lamb

cards.text: Jacob even spells it out: any goat of his that isn't speckled or spotted, or any lamb that isn't dark-colored, will be considered stolen. That's a man signing his name in PERMANENT MARKER.

cards.question: Jacob says his ___ will testify for him when Laban comes to check on his wages in the future.
Laban turns down Jacob's offer to take the speckled, spotted and dark-colored animals as his wages.

cards.text: That very day, Laban himself removes every streaked, speckled or spotted goat, every one with any white on it, and every dark-colored lamb. No sleeping on it, no circling back, THAT VERY DAY.

cards.question: Laban has pulled all the spotted and dark-colored animals out of the flocks. Whose care does he put them under?

cards.text: Then Laban puts a three-day journey between himself and Jacob. Some folks park at the far end of the lot, friend, but Laban parks THREE DAYS away.
Meanwhile, Jacob is out shepherding the rest of Laban's flocks. Then he grabs fresh branches of poplar, almond and plane trees and starts peeling off the bark, like a man with a PLAN.

cards.question: Jacob peels the bark off the fresh branches. What does that leave showing?
Jacob sets the peeled branches in the ___, right in front of the flocks.

cards.text: When the flocks are in heat and come to drink, they mate right there in front of those branches. Jacob put them where EVERYBODY has to show up, like taping your flyer to the elevator door.

cards.question: The young the flocks bear come out streaked or speckled or spotted.

cards.text: Jacob sets those streaked and spotted young apart. This man sorts sheep the way I line up chocolate chips on a cookie, EVERY ONE right where I want it.

cards.question: Jacob has set the new streaked and spotted young apart. Which animals does he make the rest of the flock face?

cards.text: Jacob also sets his own stock apart and doesn't put them with Laban's animals.
And now Jacob gets PICKY. Whenever the stronger females are in heat, he puts the branches in the troughs, in full view, so they'll breed in front of them.

cards.question: If the animals were ___, Jacob did not set out the branches.
So the weaker animals end up going to Jacob.
After all of Jacob's work with the peeled branches at the watering troughs, how do things turn out for him?

answers.text: He loses most of his flocks

cards.text: Large flocks, maidservants and menservants, camels AND donkeys. And friend, don't box this batch up yet, because Jacob's story is still in the oven.
